lines.1wbv6jl: Which AI do you use most?
lines.jdedhz: Ok! To set your baseline, you just need to write one prompt. Think of an action that you would normally do. Start with a verb like plan or edit or summarize maybe? One prompt…in your own words. “You will run this EXACT prompt in your own AI service next…”
lines.7w21jc: Are we building this primarily for your work, personal life, or both?
lines.1jwy6sj: What would you most like to stop explaining over and over in your life?
lines.1hdfsny: Do you use a different name professionally? Leave this blank if it's the same.
lines.iuxufj: How would you describe what you do?
lines.wwoa5p: What are your roles — the ones distinct enough that AI should know about each one separately?
lines.1mbyobj: What are you personally responsible for?
lines.1jfebbw: What work do you contribute to but do not own?
lines.1s9a3q: What do people sometimes assume is your responsibility, but actually isn't?
lines.f9f7qd: What kinds of decisions can you make yourself?
lines.h86y9y: What expertise do people normally come to you for?
lines.1oxeec0: Are there specific people, teams, tools, or processes worth telling AI about by name — the kind you'd expect it to recognize instead of re-explaining every time?
lines.2ernoo: Are there specific initiatives or projects underway right now that AI should know about individually — not just your general responsibilities, but named efforts with their own goals and timeline?
lines.1fgevah: When you're choosing between a fast, good-enough call and a slower, more certain one, which do you lean toward by default?
lines.l9z2xy: How much reasoning do you want to see before AI just gives you the answer?
lines.1p9hcwu: When what you've asked for is genuinely unclear, what should AI do?
lines.1fmppt6: When AI can clearly see the next step, what's your gut instinct?
lines.1m4a4r5: Do you tend to start from the big picture, or the details?
lines.3a04on: How direct should AI default to when it's writing for you?
lines.1aixhz5: How formal should the default tone be?
lines.1nj7tsj: How much should AI qualify or hedge what it tells you?
lines.1rlj7wb: Which one of these is more you?
lines.hphah1: When you need something from someone, where should the ask go?
lines.f28j20: How long should a normal answer from AI run, by default?
lines.1h9m8nq: What makes you rewrite something on sight?
lines.5287zj: Who do you write to regularly?
lines.1m97v0b: Do any of these need something noticeably different from the rest?
lines.gduznh: What terms, tools, or shorthand does your work depend on that an outsider would get wrong?
lines.1fe9zxz: Are there words or phrases you never want to see in your own writing?
lines.1gg9huw: What would you actually send a draft back over?
lines.477oqg: What should AI never do without asking you first?
lines.1vybrv3: Paste three things you wrote — as different from each other as you can find.
lines.alujyq: Now the basics: who you are and what you actually do. Not your job title — the version you'd say out loud to someone at a party. This is what AI reads first, before anything else you tell it.
lines.hdt1h7: Next: what's yours — and just as usefully, what isn't. This is the part that stops AI writing as if every call is yours to make. Two people with the same title can own completely different things. This is where you say which one you are.
lines.1yqr652: Now the names — the people, teams, and tools you mention constantly. Name them once here, and you stop explaining who they are every single time. Without this, you write: "Can you draft a note to Priya — she's my manager, she owns budget approvals, and she likes a heads-up before surprises." With it, you write: "Draft a note to Priya."
lines.1aor8h6: This one's the longest section, and the one that pays off most. These are the named projects AI can actually help you move, not just describe. Worth the extra few minutes: this is the difference between AI writing about your work and AI helping with it.
lines.41fclo: The questions get faster from here. Mostly taps, not typing. This part is about how you decide things — how fast, how certain, how much you want to be asked. Five quick picks. Under two minutes.
lines.1ql5ela: Now your voice — how things should sound when AI writes them for you. A few of these show you two versions side by side. Pick the one you'd actually send. This is the section people notice most in the results. It's why AI output stops sounding generic.
lines.dhn76p: You don't write to everyone the same way. Your manager and your team get different versions of the same update. This is where you say so. Two questions.
lines.1v2pgkf: Every workplace has its own shorthand. The acronyms, tool names, and project codenames that would lose an outsider completely. Teach it these once and you stop spelling them out mid-sentence forever.
lines.19niwtr: The rules AI doesn't get to talk itself out of. What would make you send a draft back, and what it should never do without asking you first. These stay on by default. You can turn any of them off, but most people don't.
lines.3ocqf: Last one. Paste something you wrote. One paragraph teaches AI more about your voice than every answer you've given so far. Most people who stop, stop here — with the useful part already answered and the proof still ahead. Five more minutes and you'll see it work. Then you're done — and you get to see the whole thing actually work.
lines.151r3b1: Run it once with nothing loaded. Copy your prompt — Paste and prompt — Copy and paste.
lines.1mtj9zb: Saved as your starting point. That is where you start from. Your AI wrote that with nothing about you loaded. The interview writes the file that changes it.
